title: The 3am logins
summary: Overnight SSH alerts on a Linux server: search auth.log, find the one login that worked, contain the attacker and prove how they got in.
simplification: Simplified simulation: a real brute-force run is often thousands of guesses from many addresses, so this log is cut down to stay readable. Log lines follow Ubuntu 22.04's OpenSSH and sudo formats; the IP addresses are reserved documentation ranges.

guess_root.explain: An automated tool tries a username and a password from a list. SSH is allowed through the firewall to web01 (port forward on TCP 22), so the attempt reaches the server.

cmd_sudo.explain: Inside the encrypted SSH session the attacker uses deploy's sudo rights to list root's scheduled tasks, a common first step before adding one to keep access. sudo logs every command to auth.log.

fields.explain: Lists root's scheduled tasks. Attackers check these, then often add their own to get back in later.

fields.name: Visibility
fields.explain: Network monitoring sees only SSH traffic. The command shows up on the server, in auth.log.

guided.label: Guided
guided.intro: Watch an automated SSH attack happen, guess by guess, and see the log line each step leaves behind.
guided.debrief: You've seen a brute-force login end to end, and the log lines it leaves: Invalid user, Failed password, then Accepted password. Next, predict each step in Practice mode.

practice.label: Practice
practice.intro: Same attack, but predict what happens before each step.

guess_admin.q: Three passwords for root have failed. What will an automated attack tool most likely do next?
options: Give up and move to another server
Try a different common username, like admin
Ask the server for root's password
guess_admin.why: Tools work through lists of common usernames and passwords. A refusal costs them nothing, so they just keep going.

accept_deploy.q: deploy is a real account and the password matches. What does sshd write to auth.log?
accept_deploy.why: sshd logs successes too. 'Accepted password' after a run of failures from the same address is the line every analyst looks for.

cmd_sudo.q: The attacker runs sudo crontab -l inside the SSH session. Where will that show up?
options: In auth.log, because sudo logs every command it runs
cmd_sudo.why: SSH encrypts the session on the wire, so network tools see only that a session exists. sudo writes who ran what, as whom, to auth.log on the server.

practice.debrief: You can predict each step of an SSH brute force and the evidence it leaves. Now investigate a real one in Challenge mode.

challenge.label: Challenge
challenge.intro: It's 08:05. Overnight alerts flagged unusual SSH activity on web01. Search auth.log, work out what happened, contain it, then prove the cause.

opening.say: SIEM alert on web01: lots of SSH failures overnight. Let's see what's in auth.log.
opening.log: Start: an alert says web01 saw many failed SSH logins overnight. Were they just noise, or did one get in?

hints: Start with the log viewer. Search for "Failed password" to see the guessing, and note where it came from.
Failures alone are noise on any internet-facing server. What matters is whether one worked: search for "Accepted".
deploy logged in with a password from the same address. Is that session still open? Run who.
Contain it: end the session, lock deploy so the password can't be reused, and switch SSH to keys only so guessing can't work again. Blocking the IP helps, but on its own it isn't enough.

outcomes.finding: No deploy session left: only your own analyst login is on web01.
deploy is still logged in from 203.0.113.45 (pts/0): the attacker hasn't left.
SSH now accepts keys only, so password guessing can't work.
SSH accepts passwords from anywhere the firewall lets in, so guessing can work.

outcomes.output: Rule already in place: deny 203.0.113.45 → any.

Rule added: deny 203.0.113.45 → any (new connections).
Note: a connection that's already open can carry on until it's closed.
deploy is already locked and expired.

(no output)
deploy's password is locked and the account has expired, so it can't log in again, with a password or a key.
(no output: deploy has no processes left)

(no output)
Every process owned by deploy was killed, including the attacker's shell on pts/0.

tools.label: Set PasswordAuthentication no, then reload sshd

outcomes.output: Already set. sshd is accepting keys only.

$ sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh
(config test passed, sshd reloaded)
SSH now accepts key logins only. Your own session is unaffected.

rootCause.q: web01 is contained. What let the attacker in?
options: The firewall was switched off overnight
SSH accepted passwords from the internet, and the deploy account had a guessable password
rootCause.why: The log shows plain guessing: failures for root, admin, test and oracle, then 'Accepted password for deploy' from the same address. Nothing was exploited and the firewall worked as configured: it forwarded SSH, and SSH took a weak password. Key-only logins (or no SSH from the internet) would have stopped it.
rootCause.evidenceQ: Which findings support that diagnosis? Tick the evidence, leave out what isn't.

evidence.why: The successful guess itself, and proof it was a password, not a key or an exploit.

evidence.text: auth.log: 11 'Failed password' lines from 203.0.113.45 in the minutes before
evidence.why: Shows this was guessing: one address working through usernames until one worked.
This is why guessing could work at all. With keys only, every guess fails before the password is even checked.

evidence.text: who showed deploy still logged in from 203.0.113.45
evidence.why: Confirms the attacker was still in, which shaped the response. It shows the impact rather than the cause, so it's optional here.

evidence.text: sam logged in with a key from 198.51.100.23 the evening before
evidence.why: Normal activity: a known admin, a key, a known address. Telling routine logins apart from the attack is part of the job, but it isn't evidence of the cause.
What the attacker did after getting in. Vital for the investigation (check for added cron jobs and SSH keys), but it doesn't explain how they got in.

challenge.debrief: You read auth.log the way a SOC analyst does: the failures were noise until one login worked. You ended the session, locked the account and stopped password logins, so the fix holds even if the attacker comes back from another address. Real next steps: preserve the logs, check deploy's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and every crontab for anything added, change any secrets deploy could read, and follow your incident process.

findings.finding: 11 failed passwords from 203.0.113.45 between 03:04 and 03:10, for root, admin, test, oracle and deploy.
203.0.113.45 tried usernames that don't exist (admin, test, oracle): someone guessing, not a user who forgot a password.
At 03:12:47 deploy logged in with a password from 203.0.113.45, the same address that was guessing.
sam logged in with an SSH key from 198.51.100.23 at 17:40 yesterday: a normal admin login.
At 03:14 deploy used sudo to run crontab -l as root: the attacker checking scheduled tasks.
